papers.title: Semidirect sums of tensors and the matrix multiplication exponent
papers.abstract: This note is an exposition of the recent preprints from OpenAI that establish the bound $\omega \leq 9/4$ on the matrix multiplication exponent. We argue that the heart of these preprints is a new technique, which we formulate as the untwisting lemma for semidirect sums of tensors. This gives a generally applicable method for analyzing tensors. We also discuss further consequences of this method, as well as the relation between the OpenAI proof and previous work.

papers.title: Entropy-Weighted Soundness for Multi-Answer Birthday Graphs
papers.abstract: The vertices of a Boolean birthday graph are partial assignments on $\ell$-subsets of $n$ variables. Although a satisfying assignment induces a $K$-clique for $K=\binom n\ell$, an arbitrary selection of $K$ vertices may repeat some views and omit others. This makes soundness substantially harder than under uniform view sampling. For bounded-occurrence, constant-gap Boolean ternary CSPs whose constraints each involve three distinct variables (allowing arbitrary Boolean predicates), we prove that the graph's maximum induced $K$-vertex density satisfies \[ \rho^*(K)\le 2\exp\!\left(-c\, \frac{\ell^3}{n^2\log(en/\ell)}\right) \] for $2\le\ell\le x_0n$ and $\ell\log(en/\ell)\ge C_0\log(n+1)$, with positive constants depending only on the source parameters. The argument refines the biclique counting method by charging the entropy of an adversarially chosen flattening to mutual information and a combinatorial obstruction energy. In the overlapping parameter range it strengthens the explicit soundness exponent previously established for this graph. We also establish an unconditional stability theorem for arbitrary sets $H$ of exactly $K$ distinct local assignments, with missing views and multiple answers: $f_*(H)\le34(n/\ell)q_{\mathrm{con}}(H)$ for every $1\le\ell\le n$. It gives a complementary additive near-clique soundness bound. We do not derive a new fine-grained hardness theorem.

papers.title: Abelian embeddings make useful promises: approximation of detrivialised equations
papers.abstract: We study the following family of search problems: given a system of equations $x+y+z\equiv 0\pmod p$ promised to admit a solution that is nonconstant on every equation, find a $c$-colouring of the variables that makes no equation monochromatic. For $p\in\{2,3\}$, the problem recovers known tractable Promise Constraint Satisfaction Problems (PCSPs). For $p > 3$, we obtain a complete complexity classification: the problem is polynomial-time solvable for $c \geq 4$, yet even its decision version is NP-hard for $c = 3$, and it is not well-defined for $c = 2$. Our main conceptual contribution is a general tractability framework for PCSPs based on Abelian embeddings, a notion introduced by Bhangale, Khot, and Minzer [STOC 2022] in the study of quantitative approximation of satisfiable CSPs. We show that suitable Abelian embeddings yield polynomial-time PCSP reductions realised by singleton algorithms in the sense of Zhuk [FOCS 2026]. On the hardness side, the promise relation is far removed from the reconfigurable regime covered by the conditional hardness framework of Banakh, Barsukov, and Nakajima [LICS 2026]; our proof instead relies on a new additive-combinatorial rigidity theorem classifying special $3$-colourings of $\mathbb{Z}_p$.

papers.title: Geometric Bin Packing Beyond Convexity: Approximation Schemes without Augmentation
papers.abstract: We study the geometric bin packing problem for simple polygonal regions, i.e., non-degenerate, connected, rational regions, in the minimum number of unit-square bins, allowing only translations. We even consider packing general non-convex objects, possibly with holes, where we can then pack smaller objects. Previous schemes cover squares (MOR'06), circles and other $L_p$-balls (Algorithmica'16), sufficiently skewed rectangles (Algorithmica'23), and convex fat objects with a constant number of distinct shapes under resource augmentation (arXiv'24, WAOA'23). The result for circles and other $L_p$-balls needs bin augmentation to obtain rational packing realizations. For restricted classes of $L$-shaped polygons, Gerlach et al. (SoCG'26) give constant worst-case guarantees, while for general non-convex objects, bounding-box reductions give just approximation factors that depend on fatness. Against this background, we present a general framework that provides asymptotic polynomial-time approximation schemes (APTAS) for bin packing of any fixed class of simple polygonal regions satisfying just two assumptions. First, covering any object by the grid cells intersecting its interior in any sufficiently fine square grid, relative to the object's bounding box, increases its area by at most a small fraction. Second, the class can be partitioned into a constant number of sequences such that each object in a sequence can be translated to fit inside every preceding object. In particular, certain classes of star-shaped polygons and more general polygonal regions, including some with simple holes, satisfy both assumptions. In addition, our framework does not require a bound on the objects' boundary complexity. We emphasize that our results require no bin augmentation whatsoever and yield explicit, exact rational packings of polynomial encoding length for all input objects.

papers.title: A King for Almost Everyone
papers.abstract: A tournament is an orientation of a complete graph. A vertex $v$ controls a vertex $u\neq v$ if there is a directed path of length at most two from $v$ to $u$, and a $\delta$-king is one that controls at least $\delta(n-1)$ vertices. In the query complexity model, each query reveals the orientation of an edge. Shen, Sheng and Wu [SICOMP'03] established an $\Omega(n^{4/3})$ lower bound on the deterministic query complexity of finding a $1$-king, and a non-matching upper bound of $O(n^{3/2})$. Neither bound has been improved in over two decades, despite substantial progress on variants of the problem. For $\delta$-kings with $\delta < 1$, Biswas, Jayapaul, Raman and Satti [Discrete Applied Mathematics'22] showed that $O(n^{4/3})$ queries suffice to find a $\frac12$-king. Lachish, Reidl and Trehan [FSTTCS'22] improved this guarantee to $\frac12+\frac{2}{17}$ using $\widetilde{O}(n^{4/3})$ queries, and asked whether a larger fraction could be achieved within the same query bound. We answer this question affirmatively for every fixed fraction below one: for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, we give a deterministic algorithm that finds a $(1-\varepsilon)$-king using $O(n^{4/3})$ queries. The design of our algorithm is informed by a structural analysis combining a sparse regularity lemma due to Allen, Kohayakawa, Mota and Parente [Electronic Journal of Combinatorics'14] with a new sampling argument based on a reachability theorem of Afek, Gafni and Linial [arXiv'19].

papers.title: On the optimality of truncation among binary linear sketches
papers.abstract: We study statistical inference and function evaluation problems in which the input binary vector is available only through a binary linear sketch, i.e., a fixed number of parity measurements. We show that under a certain monotonicity condition, simply truncating the input by retaining a subset of its coordinates is optimal among all linear sketches of the same size. In particular, this applies to distributed testing of correlations of binary vectors when they are of opposite signs and evaluating unate Boolean functions on uniformly random inputs. Additionally, given that truncation is optimal, we immediately have lower bounds for arbitrary binary linear sketches. To illustrate this application, we consider the one-way communication complexity of a distributional graph connectivity problem on $n$ vertices and show that truncation, and hence all binary linear sketches, requires $\Theta(n \log n)$ bits to achieve constant error, while a nonlinear protocol only requires $O(\log n)$ bits.

papers.title: State Evolution and Universality of Iterated Linear Programs for the Binary Perceptron
papers.abstract: The binary perceptron is a random constraint satisfaction problem that asks for a sign vector satisfying a system of random linear inequalities. Its solution space has a strikingly extreme geometry: at every positive constraint density, all but a vanishing fraction of the solutions are isolated. Yet polynomial-time algorithms find solutions at small enough constraint density, which raises the question of how efficient algorithms navigate such a landscape. Linear programming is a natural algorithm to study here, but its analysis has so far been limited to a single round. Li, Schramm, and Zhou (STOC 2025) analyzed one linear program followed by iterative rounding. In this work, we overcome this limitation and give a precise analysis of iterated linear programming for the binary perceptron. (1) For Gaussian matrices and any fixed number of rounds, we characterize the iterated linear programs exactly through a deterministic state-evolution recursion. (2) Adding a final rounding step, we obtain a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for the binary perceptron. Numerical evaluations of the recursion provide evidence that it succeeds at constraint density $\alpha=0.60$ with zero margin, well beyond the range $\alpha\le0.1$ guaranteed by the single-LP analysis and $\alpha\approx0.327$ (Jo and Lee, 2026), the best guarantee so far. (3) We establish universality, showing that the same characterization holds for matrices with i.i.d. entries drawn from any centered, unit-variance subgaussian law. The key idea of our proof is that, although conditioning on earlier rounds makes the matrix non-Gaussian, its conditional law can be computed explicitly and remains close to a Gaussian law, so the convex Gaussian min-max theorem applies in every round. For universality, we compare Gaussian and subgaussian matrices through the Lindeberg principle, using a regularized version of each linear program.

papers.title: Gaussian Difference Dynamics: Breaking the $2^{n/2}$ Barrier for the Shortest Vector Problem and Discrete Gaussian Sampling
papers.abstract: We give classical randomized algorithms in a word RAM model that break the $2^{n/2}$ barrier for both discrete Gaussian sampling (DGS) and the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP). For every fixed $\alpha>1$, shifted DGS on arbitrary lattices at width $\sigma\ge\alpha\eta_{1/2}(L)$ takes $$ (3/2)^{n/2+o(n)}\text{ time} \qquad\text{and}\qquad (4/3)^{n/2+o(n)}\text{ space}. $$ These bounds match the Becker--Ducas--Gama--Laarhoven (BDGL) heuristic sieving exponents. At widths at least $3\eta_{1/2}(L)/2$, the same total cost suffices for an entire batch of $\lfloor(4/3)^{n/2}\rfloor$ samples jointly close to independent target Gaussians. For SVP on arbitrary lattices, our algorithm returns a shortest nonzero vector with high probability in $$ 2^{0.4130n+o(n)}\text{ time} \qquad\text{and}\qquad 2^{0.3138n+o(n)}\text{ space}. $$ As a corollary, we obtain centered DGS at every width with the same exponents, answering a question of Stephens-Davidowitz (SODA 2016). We introduce Gaussian difference dynamics (GDD), a framework for tracking expected counts and pairwise clustering of vectors through repeated differencing. A closed recursion for the first two counting moments controls these quantities relative to a Gaussian reference, without requiring independence within intermediate lists. Accurate moment bounds let us extract a Gaussian sample by weighted selection, while the weaker bounds needed to establish a shortest vector representation allow us to retain more differences. We perform these transitions on thin spherical shells, where the Gaussian rejection weights can be renormalized at subexponential cost. For batch sampling, we combine this geometry with the double rejection technique of Doulgerakis and Laarhoven to control the joint distribution of outputs while reusing vectors.

papers.title: Space-Optimal Algorithms for Spanning Forests in Dynamic Streams at Every Confidence Level: With and Without Deletion Constraints
papers.abstract: We characterize the optimal space for one-pass spanning-forest computation in dynamic streams of $v$-vertex simple graphs with failure probability at most $\delta$. Nelson and Yu proved an $\Omega(v\log^2v\log(v/\delta))$-bit lower bound, establishing the AGM algorithm's optimality for each fixed $0<\epsilon<1$ and $2^{-v^{1-\epsilon}}<\delta\le1/4$. We resolve the remaining high-confidence regime: for every $0<\delta\le1/4$, matching lower bounds and an algorithm give \[ \Theta\!\left(\min\left\{v^2,\;v\log(v/\delta)\log^2\!\left(2+\frac{v}{\log(v/\delta)}\right)\right\}\right) \] bits, improving space by up to a factor of $\Theta((\log v/\log\log v)^2)$ in this regime. We also study streams with at most $Z$ previously inserted edges deleted and not yet reinserted at report time, where the integer $Z\ge0$ is given in advance. Total deletions, restorations, and intermediate absence counts are unrestricted. For a single report and every $0<\delta\le1/4$, matching lower bounds and a one-pass randomized algorithm yield optimal space $\Theta(\mathcal L(v,Z,\log(1/\delta)))$ bits, where $x_Z(t)=\min\{Z+1,v,\sqrt{vt}\}$ and \[ \mathcal L(v,Z,t)=v\log v\min\{\log^2v,\log^2(Z+2)\} +vt\log\!\left(1+\frac{x_Z(t)}t\right)\log\!\left(1+\frac v{x_Z(t)}\right). \] At zero error, a lower bound for all zero-error algorithms and a matching deterministic algorithm give optimal space \[ \Theta\!\left(\min\{v^2,v(Z+1)\log(1+v/(Z+1))\}\right) \] bits. Together, these results characterize the memory required across all confidence levels and report-time edge-loss bounds.

papers.title: Binary Huffman Coding with Unequal Letter Costs Is NP-Complete
papers.abstract: Binary prefix coding assigns prefix-free binary words to symbols to minimize their frequency-weighted cost. Huffman solved the equal-letter-cost case in polynomial time in 1952 [Proc. IRE'52]. For unequal letter costs, Karp gave an integer-programming formulation in 1961 [IRE Trans. Inf. Theory'61]. Exact polynomial-time algorithms for fixed integer costs were given by Golin and Rote [IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory'98] and Bradford, Golin, Larmore, and Rytter [J. Algorithms'02]. For input-dependent costs, Golin, Mathieu, and Young gave a polynomial-time approximation scheme [SICOMP'12]. The exact complexity when letter costs are part of the input had remained unresolved. We resolve this $65$-year-old problem by proving that deciding whether there exists a binary prefix-free code of frequency-weighted cost at most a given threshold is NP-complete, even when the letter costs are consecutive positive integers $(M,M+1)$ supplied as part of the input. All frequencies, letter costs, and thresholds are encoded in binary. Consequently, finding an optimal code is NP-hard. Our proof uses two polynomial-time reductions, starting from Planar Independent Set. The intermediate problem prescribes the number of leaves at each depth of a full ordered binary tree and minimizes a signed linear score on their sorted right-edge counts. The first reduction represents an independent-set verification program by a tree growing level by level. A fixed-profile identity converts narrow coordinate restrictions into linear penalties that enforce the computation. The second reduction adds large dyadic terms to the symbol frequencies to force prescribed depths. These terms contribute a constant to the weighted number of ones, leaving smaller signed perturbations to reproduce the tree score.

papers.title: Differentially Oblivious Priority Queues with Sublogarithmic Cost
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study exact online integer priority queues under differential obliviousness in the balls-and-bins model. Given a public upper bound $T$ on the number of operations and assuming that the priorities are bounded by a polynomial in $T$, we construct an $(\eps,\delta)$-differentially oblivious priority queue supporting insertion and minimum extraction, which requires $\polylog(T)$ private memory. For constant $\varepsilon>0$ and $\delta=\exp(-\Theta(\log^2 T))$, our construction incurs $O(\log T/\log\log T)$ expected amortized total work per operation, which breaks the $\Omega(\log T)$ barrier for fully oblivious priority queues~[Jacob et al., SODA'2019]. Further, we prove a matching lower bound for $(\eps,\delta)$-differentially oblivious priority queues with $\varepsilon=O(1)$ and $\delta=o(1)$, which indicates that our construction is asymptotically optimal in terms of total work.

papers.title: The Power of Bidegeneracy for Hypergraph Data Structures
papers.abstract: A hypergraph $H = (V,E)$ describes a set system over a vertex universe $V$. Hypergraphs are increasingly popular in network science, as they represent interactions between subsets of vertices. A natural challenge is to design a data structure for $H$ to quickly answer basic questions about it, e.g. how many neighbors a vertex $v$ has or whether a hyperedge contains a vertex subset $S$. Such questions are trivial for graphs, for which we simply inspect the adjacency list. The gold standard, from a data structures perspective, would be near-linear time preprocessing and query answering in (poly)logarithmic time. Since this is unlikely for arbitrary $H$, we ask for well-motivated hypergraph properties that can make such a goal possible. We introduce bidegeneracy, a measure of hypergraph sparsity that strictly generalizes many other measures, including bounded degree, bounded rank, and bounded $\infty$-degeneracy. We show that bounded bidegeneracy yields fast hypergraph data structures. For a large set of fundamental queries, including their listing and sampling versions, we obtain near-linear preprocessing and (poly)logarithmic query time. Moreover, direct reductions from assumptions like the Orthogonal Vectors Conjecture suggest that, without assumptions on the input, these structures require almost-quadratic preprocessing or almost-linear query time. We use bidegeneracy to compute a compressed representation of $H$ and perform careful reductions to stabbing and searching problems in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Our framework significantly extends the well-studied "partial matching" problem of finding database entries through wildcard search. It also uncovers an intriguing connection between hypergraph sparsity, compression, and the complexity of hypergraph primitives. We also find remarkably low bidegeneracy in hypergraph datasets from the literature, suggesting practical consequences.

papers.title: Faster Planar Diameter using Pseudoline Envelopes
papers.abstract: We give an improved algorithm for weighted directed planar diameter that runs in $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ time. This improves upon the $\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})$ time algorithm for weighted directed planar diameter of Gawrychowski, Kaplan, Mozes, Sharir, and Weimann [SIAM J. Comput. 2021] and the recent $\widetilde{O}(n^{8/5})$ time algorithm for unweighted undirected planar diameter of Fredslund-Hansen, Mozes, and Weimann [SOSA 2027]. The main new result is an improved data structure for computing the farthest vertex when given feasible planar distances to the vertices on the outer face. The critical insight is the fact that normalized distances to the vertices of a face behave like pseudolines, for which we can leverage range searching and upper envelope data structures. Using the farthest vertex data structure, we are able to compute all vertex eccentricities and diameter in $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$.

papers.title: The Power of Interaction in Locally Edge-Private Subgraph Counting
papers.abstract: We study (non-induced) subgraph counting under interactive local edge differential privacy (LEDP). Given a fixed pattern graph $H$ with $k$ vertices, $\ell\ge1$ edges, and $q$ connected components, our goal is to approximately count its copies in an arbitrary $n$-vertex undirected graph while preserving edge privacy. We give two complementary accuracy guarantees. First, for every $H$, we give Linear Noise Cancellation (LNC), a two-round $\varepsilon$-LEDP algorithm with additive error and root mean square error both $O(n^{k-3/2}/\varepsilon^\ell)$ on every $n$-vertex graph. For fixed sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, this improves the optimal noninteractive additive error for triangles by a factor of $\sqrt n$ and gives the same improvement in worst-case root mean square error for all cliques on at least three vertices. To our knowledge, this is the first separation between interactive and noninteractive LEDP subgraph counting, showing that a single additional round can improve worst-case accuracy polynomially. Second, we determine how accuracy improves when the graph has maximum degree at most a public bound $d$. Our Predict and Correct (PC) framework gives an $(\ell+2)$-round $\varepsilon$-LEDP algorithm with additive error $O(n^{q-1/2}d^{k-q-1}\log^{3\ell-2}n/\varepsilon^\ell)$. For connected patterns, its polynomial factor is $\sqrt n\,d^{k-2}$, giving sublinear error on constant-degree graphs at fixed privacy. We prove matching lower bounds in $n$ and $d$, up to logarithmic factors at fixed privacy, even under arbitrary interaction and approximate privacy with sufficiently small $\delta$. At $d=\Theta(n)$, the lower bound also establishes the optimality of LNC's dependence on $n$.

papers.title: Finding Hypercliques Faster Than Brute Force
papers.abstract: We show that for any fixed $k$, there exists $\varepsilon_k > 0$ such that, given a $(k-1)$-uniform hypergraph $H$ on $n$ vertices, one can count the number of $k$-hypercliques in $H$ in $O(n^{k-\varepsilon_k})$ time. This refutes the hyperclique conjecture of Lincoln, Vassilevska Williams, and Williams (SODA 2018). Our result follows from the uniform construction of a family of arithmetic circuits of size $O(n^{k-\varepsilon_k})$ for the $k$-hyperclique tensor, a natural higher-order generalization of the matrix multiplication tensor. We obtain two corollaries. First, for every $k$, there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that Max-$k$SAT can be solved in $2^{(1-\varepsilon)n} \cdot \mathrm{poly}(m,n)$ time. Second, for every $k$, there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that arithmetic progressions of length $k$ in subsets of $\{0,1,\ldots,n\}$ can be detected in $n^{2-\varepsilon}$ time. Both corollaries refute other prominent conjectures in the literature.

papers.title: Agnostic Learning by Imitating
papers.abstract: Given a class of machine learning models and sample access to a data distribution with binary labels, which computational task is harder: training a discriminative model that distinguishes positive and negative labels as well as the best member of the class, or training a generative model whose outputs are indistinguishable from real data by all members of the class? We prove that these two fundamental tasks in computational learning theory are not just closely related, but actually equivalent to each other in complexity. One direction of this equivalence was previously known. Indeed, the powerful regularity lemma in complexity theory gives an efficient oracle reduction from the indistinguishability task (a.k.a. multiaccuracy) to the distinguishing task (a.k.a. agnostic learning) in the style of boosting algorithms. Our main contribution is an efficient oracle reduction in the other direction. Taking this idea further, we show that a multiaccuracy oracle is a remarkably powerful primitive, achieving not just agnostic learning but also a wide range of seemingly more demanding learning objectives via similarly efficient and direct constructions. Our results crucially use the power of making adaptive queries to the oracle, and stand in stark contrast to prior work, which showed that post-processing a single multiaccurate predictor is insufficient for even weak forms of learning. On a technical level, we draw a connection between our (offline) problem and a version of no-regret learning in the online setting, which allows us to use follow-the-leader type algorithms to modify the label distribution and aggregate the predictions of the multiaccuracy oracle.

papers.title: Breaking the quantum barriers for Graph Collision
papers.abstract: In the graph collision problem, the task is to decide whether a known graph on $n$ vertices contains an edge with both endpoints marked, given query access to the input bits specifying the marked vertices. We first refute the conjectured $\Omega(n^{2/3})$ query lower bound with a bounded error quantum algorithm using $\widetilde O(n^{92/139})$ queries. We then refine this approach to obtain a $\widetilde O(n^{11/17})$ query algorithm. We also obtain a $\widetilde O((nq)^{11/17})$ query bound for all (partial) Boolean output functions with positive certificate complexity at most 2 and alphabet size $q$, contrasting a known $\Omega(n^{2/3})$ lower bound for such problems with large alphabet sizes. We complement these algorithms with an $\Omega(\sqrt{n\log n})$ quantum query lower bound for graph collision, exceeding the $O(\sqrt n)$ certificate complexity barrier for the positive adversary method.

papers.title: Scalable Exact Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering via Sparse Geographic Distance Graphs
papers.abstract: Exact hierarchical agglomerative clustering (HAC) of large spatial datasets is limited in practice by the $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ time and memory required for the full pairwise distance matrix. We present GSHAC (Geographically Sparse Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering), a system that makes exact HAC feasible at scales of millions of geographic features on a commodity workstation. GSHAC replaces the distance matrix with a sparse geographic distance graph containing only pairs within a user-specified geodesic bound $h_{\max}$, constructed in $\mathcal{O}(n \cdot k)$ time via spatial indexing, where $k$ is the mean number of neighbors within $h_{\max}$. Connected components of this graph define independent subproblems, and we prove that the resulting assignments are exact for all standard linkage methods at any cut height $h \le h_{\max}$. For single linkage, an MST-based path keeps memory at $\mathcal{O}(n_k + m_k)$ per component. Applied to a global mining inventory ($n = 261{,}073$), the system completes in 12 s (109 MiB peak HAC memory) versus $\approx 545$ GiB for the dense baseline. On a 2-million-point GeoNames sample, all tested thresholds completed in under 3 minutes with peak memory under 3 GiB. We provide a scikit-learn-compatible implementation for direct integration into GIS workflows.

papers.title: Dense Language Generation Made Simple: Deterministic, Randomized, and Multi-Order Algorithms
papers.abstract: Language generation in the limit is a theoretical framework for studying how a generator can learn to produce new valid strings from a stream of positive examples. In this model, an adversary chooses an unknown language from a countable family and enumerates its elements in an arbitrary order, while the generator must eventually output only elements of the language that have not yet appeared in the enumeration. Reliable generation is thus formalized through two eventual guarantees: validity and novelty relative to the observed data. To further quantify the breadth of the generator's outputs, Kleinberg and Wei (FOCS 2025, STOC 2026) introduced lower density as a measure of output coverage. Given an order representing the importance or relevance of possible outputs, lower density is the asymptotic lower bound, as $n$ grows, on the fraction of the first $n$ elements of the target language that the generator outputs before they appear in the data. Kleinberg and Wei showed that $1/2$ is the optimal lower-density guarantee for deterministic algorithms. We develop a simple and unified framework for obtaining optimal lower-density guarantees. We first give a deterministic algorithm that recovers the optimal guarantee of $1/2$ with a significantly simpler analysis than prior work. We then demonstrate the flexibility of our framework through two extensions. First, against an oblivious adversary, randomization raises the optimal guarantee to $1-1/e$. Second, for any finite collection of orders, the optimal deterministic and randomized guarantees can be achieved simultaneously with respect to every order, so accommodating multiple notions of importance or relevance entails no loss in the optimal guarantee.

papers.title: A Near-Linear Element-Kernel for \(d\)-Hitting Set
papers.abstract: In \(d\)-Hitting Set, the input consists of a finite universe \(U\), a family \(\mathcal S\) of subsets of \(U\) with size at most \(d\), and an integer \(k\). The task is to decide whether at most \(k\) elements of \(U\) can intersect every set in \(\mathcal S\). Previously known kernels contain \(O(k^{d-1})\) elements and \(O(k^d)\) sets. Whether the number of elements can be reduced to \(O(k^{d-1-\varepsilon})\) for some constant \(\varepsilon>0\) is a longstanding open problem in kernelization. In this paper, we answer this question affirmatively by giving a near-linear randomized element-kernel and a subquadratic deterministic element-kernel through a re-encoding of the instance. For every fixed \(d\geq3\), we give a one-sided randomized kernel with \(O_d(k\log^3k)\) elements and a deterministic kernel with \(O_d(k^{7/4}\log^{3/2}k)\) elements. Our kernels may still contain \(k^{O(d)}\) sets and the parameter \(k\) may grow polynomially.

papers.title: An FPRAS for Counting Common Bases of Two Matroids
papers.abstract: We design the first fully polynomial-time randomized approximation scheme ($\mathsf{FPRAS}$) for approximately counting and uniformly sampling common bases of two matroids given by their independence oracles. Moreover, our algorithms generalize far beyond this to Hadamard products of two probability measures on the Boolean cube satisfying a simple nonnegative curvature condition. These algorithmic primitives have myriad applications in statistical physics, polyhedral combinatorics, the theory of quantum many-body systems, and beyond. The central difficulty is that the hard constraints imposed by the two input matroids (or the two input measures, more generally) obstruct traditional approaches based on local Markov chains. Relaxing these constraints can restore rapid mixing, but configurations that satisfy the original hard constraints may become exponentially rare if this is done na\"ively. Our main contribution is a novel approach for approximate counting that marries Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) with convex programming to overcome these obstacles: - We relax the intersection by imposing an overlap penalty on the product measure formed by the two input measures. We prove, via an integrated Bochner-type method, that this "soft intersection" satisfies a Poincar\'e Inequality uniformly over all external fields. - We use samples from the relaxed distribution to solve a dual maximum entropy convex program inspired by the Gurvits capacity. This program reweights the soft intersection measure using external fields to boost the aggregate probability of configurations satisfying the hard intersection constraint, without changing their relative weights. We bound the success probability directly using the uniform Poincar\'e Inequality and smallness of the gradient norm. AI Disclosure: GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra and GPT-6 Astra Ultra were heavily used to develop the ideas in this paper.

papers.title: Nearly optimal Personalized PageRank computation
papers.abstract: We study the fundamental problem of computing Personalized PageRank (PPR) on an undirected and unweighted graph $G$. We focus on the $\eps$-error guarantee introduced by Andersen, Chung, and Lang [ACL; FOCS 2006 $\&$ Internet Math 2007]. Their classic local push method computes an approximate PPR vector satisfying the ACL $\eps$-error guarantee in $O((\alpha\eps)^{-1})$ time, where $\alpha$ is the teleportation parameter. This problem has a lower bound $\Omega(\eps^{-1})$. Working with idealized SDDM solves, we eliminate the dependence on $\alpha$ and present an algorithm that achieves the same error guarantee in $O(\eps^{-1-o(1)})$ time. Consequently, we obtain a nearly optimal algorithm for PPR computation under the ACL error guarantee, and a nearly linear algorithm for local graph clustering with complexity independent of $\phi$.

papers.title: Unconditional Boolean Dynamic Lower Bounds from Disjointness
papers.abstract: We prove an unconditional $\Omega((\log n/\log\log n)^2)$ lower bound on the maximum of the worst-case update time and expected query time for the insert-only version of Patrascu's multiphase Disjointness problem [STOC 2010]. The bound holds in the zero-error cell-probe model with logarithmic word size. Patrascu's reductions transfer it to directed reachability under edge insertions, already on directed acyclic graphs of depth $2$. This improves the $\widetilde{\Omega}(\log^{3/2} n)$ bound of Larsen and Yu [SICOMP 2025] to the quadratic-logarithmic scale previously attained for dynamic range counting and multiphase Inner Product. The bound also transfers to a broad collection of dynamic graph, algebraic, geometric, and string problems. We also obtain a separation between amortized and worst-case time for streaming regular-expression membership. For a simple family of expressions of maximum length $M$ over a polynomial-size alphabet, a deterministic algorithm uses $O(1)$ amortized time per symbol on every input stream, whereas every zero-error cell-probe algorithm with word size $w=\Theta(\log M)$ requires $\Omega((\log M/\log\log M)^2)$ time on some symbol. The proof adapts Ko's 2.5-round multiphase communication framework [FOCS 2026] from Inner Product to Disjointness. Our main technical observation is that the protocol's verification step allows a one-sided corruption bound to replace the discrepancy property used for Inner Product.

papers.title: A Linear Lower Bound for Convex Body Chasing in Every Norm
papers.abstract: We establish an $\Omega(d)$ lower bound on the competitive ratio of convex body chasing in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with movement costs measured in any norm. Previously, the best known lower bound valid across all norms was $\Omega(d^{1/6})$, established by Papazov (2023); stronger lower bounds were known for $\ell_p$ norms, where Bubeck, Klartag, Lee, Li, and Sellke (2019) had established a lower bound of $\Omega(\max\{\sqrt{d}, d^{1-1/p}\})$. In particular, a linear lower bound was known only for the $\ell_\infty$ norm, realized by the standard construction of chasing faces of a hypercube. Our lower bound strictly improves on the prior universal and $\ell_p$ lower bounds for $p < \infty$ and shows that the functional Steiner point algorithm of Sellke (2023) - which has competitive ratio $O(d)$ - is asymptotically optimal for every norm. Our approach is based on the recursive construction of Bubeck, Coester, and Rabani (2023) for metrical service systems, which gives a lower bound of $\Omega(r^2)$ for requests of size $O(r)$. We show that requests in their construction, each comprising a set of discrete points in a graph metric, can be mapped to the vertices of convex requests in a $(2r+1)$-dimensional $\ell_p$ vector space while approximately preserving movement costs up to a factor of $O(r)$; the general result then follows via Milman's (1985) quotient-of-a-subspace theorem.

papers.title: Tight Coreset Bounds for $(k,z)$-Clustering in Euclidean and Doubling Metrics
papers.abstract: We determine the optimal worst-case size of strong coresets for $(k,z)$-clustering in Euclidean spaces and doubling metrics, up to polylogarithmic factors. In Euclidean space, previous lower bounds matched the best upper bounds only for $\varepsilon\gtrsim k^{-1/(z+2)}$. We close the gap for arbitrarily small $\varepsilon$, establishing the optimal size $\widetilde\Theta(\min\{k^{(2z+2)/(z+2)}\varepsilon^{-2},\,k\varepsilon^{-z-2}\})$ for every fixed $z\ge1$, all $k\ge1$, and $0<\varepsilon<1$. Our lower bound replaces each offset in a previous hard instance by a group of distinct offsets. A fixed family of $k$-center queries and four-wise independent signs force a large relative cost error for every sufficiently small subset with arbitrary nonnegative weights. For doubling metrics of dimension $D$, we resolve the previously unmatched bounds for $z>2$. We prove an upper bound of $\widetilde O(k^{2-2/z}D\varepsilon^{-2})$ and a lower bound that, together with known upper bounds, establishes the optimal size $\widetilde\Theta(kD\min\{k^{1-2/z}\varepsilon^{-2},\,\varepsilon^{-z}\})$ for fixed $z>2$, $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_z$, and $D\ge C_z\log(2/\varepsilon)$, where $C_z>0$ and $\varepsilon_z\in(0,1)$ depend only on $z$. The lower bound exploits the ability to encode $\Theta(D)$ independent signs per center without diluting relative cost discrepancy. For the upper bound, we use independent, unbiased two-point summaries that exactly preserve cluster mass and anchor cost, combined with iterative size reduction.

papers.title: A Family of Well-Behaved Multiflow Instances
papers.abstract: We introduce a family of cut-sufficient instances for undirected multiflow that generalizes single-source planar and fully-planar instances. We also show the family has an additive $6 d_{\max}$ error for converting a fractional flow into an unsplittable one.

papers.title: The Hyperclique Hypothesis is False
papers.abstract: The Hyperclique Hypothesis postulates that, for all constants $k > h \geq 3$, detecting a $k$-clique in an $h$-uniform hypergraph with $n$ vertices requires time $n^{k-o(1)}$. This hypothesis is false: there is an algebraic algorithm that detects (and even counts) $k$-cliques in $h$-uniform hypergraphs in time $O(n^{(1-\epsilon_h)k})$. Via known reductions, this also refutes the recently proposed $k$-AP Hypothesis. As a consequence, many problems with conditional lower bounds based on these two hypotheses may admit faster algorithms after all. This result is almost entirely due to AI.

papers.title: A Constant-Factor Approximation for Capacitated Facility Location with Outliers
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic polynomial-time $(60/11+\eps)$-approximation for metric capacitated facility location with outliers, with arbitrary opening costs and nonuniform hard capacities. The algorithm respects both capacities and the outlier budget. Its guarantee, approximately $5.455$, is close to the best known factor $5+\eps$ for capacitated facility location without outliers. The main ingredient is a local-search comparison for a common rejection penalty that retains the signed difference between the algorithm's and the comparator's rejection counts. Ordinary approximation guarantees for the penalty objective do not provide this comparison. We extend the exchange-forest accounting of Bansal, Garg, and Gupta \cite{BGG18} so that a nonnegative assignment remainder pays for rejection and cancels in the final bound. We then merge two penalty assignments whose served counts bracket the outlier quota. Grouping alternating paths by their terminal facility preserves capacities and shares opening costs. These ingredients give a $(20/3+\eps)$-approximation; starting each penalty run from the preceding solution improves the guarantee to $60/11+\eps$.

papers.title: Incremental Open Addressing Has No Time-Space Tradeoff
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that there is no time-space tradeoff in incremental open addressing: there is an incremental open-addressed hash table that supports $O(1)$ worst-case expected time insertions, positive queries, and negative queries, at any load factor (even load factor $1$). As an intermediate result, we also revisit the problem of constructing an incremental open-addressed hash table that does not perform reordering (does not move elements around over time). In this setting, we show that it is possible to get $O(1)$ amortized expected positive query time together with $O(1)$ worst-case expected insertion time, a combination that was not previously known to be possible.

papers.title: Online Metric Matching with Unknown i.i.d. Arrivals
papers.abstract: We study online metric matching with $n$ servers and $n$ requests drawn independently from an unknown distribution. Each request must be matched immediately and irrevocably to an unused server, and the algorithm receives no samples before the process starts. We give a randomized algorithm that is $O((\log\log\log n)^2)$-competitive on arbitrary metric spaces and $O(1)$-competitive on tree metrics. These guarantees match the corresponding bounds for known i.i.d. request distributions in [GGPW19] up to constant factors. More generally, our competitive ratio is $O(\alpha(n))$ whenever the Fair-Bias algorithm introduced in that work has competitive ratio $\alpha(n)$ for known i.i.d. arrivals on the same class of metrics. Consequently, proving that Fair-Bias is constant-competitive on general metrics would also yield a constant-competitive algorithm for unknown i.i.d. arrivals.
